transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-09-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Recording: https://ff-recordings.example/ff-20250902-7a3b (auto)
Attendees: Michael Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Nina Patel (Redwood CSM); Jules Martin, Amira Khan, Luis Ortega, Tara Singh (Sable Finance)

Summary:
Quick demo focused on audit log sanitization, console toggles for request storage, and API flags for PII masking. Customer wants to understand retention tiers, how audit logs are sanitized for internal compliance, and what controls are available to prevent sensitive data being persisted. Agreed to a short POC with trial tenant and follow-up security session.

Topics: audit logs, scrubbing rules, retention windows, KMS integration, console toggle, api flag (redact_user_data / pii_masking), compliance check, rollback and revertability of logs

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Michael: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate it. Uh we wanted to show the console flows and API toggles you asked about for audit logs and request storage. I'm Michael Chen, AE, and Priya will run the live bits.
[00:09] Jules: Thanks Michael, yeah we're mostly curious how the logs are sanitized at ingest and what parts of the request ever touch long term storage, mm-hmm.
[00:15] Priya: Great question. We'll start in the Console — top-level setting is under Settings -> Data & Logs -> Request Storage. You get three tiers: off, ephemeral (7d), and long (90d). That map's what you saw in the doc but I'll also show the API flags, which is useful if you want SDK-level control per call.
[00:31] Amira: When you say 'ephemeral' is that encrypted at rest? And are audit logs separated from request payloads?
[00:36] Priya: Yes both tiers are encrypted at rest with customer KMS options for Private; hosted accounts use Redwood-managed KMS unless you bind your own. Audit logs are a meta-layer — they record metadata about calls for observability (time, model, latency) and they never contain full prompt bodies unless request storage is enabled. So when request_storage=off you still get the audit event but no payload.
[00:54] Luis: Is there a scrub step before anything hits even ephemeral storage? Like automatic PII redaction?
[00:59] Priya: We have two layers. First, automatic heuristics that mask obvious PII (SSNs, credit cards, emails) using a regex-and-ml hybrid. Second, configurable scrubbing rules — in Console you can add field-level scrubs or regex rules, and those run before writing to storage. So for ephemeral we still run scrubs. For long retention you can also enable a "sanitization + redact" pipeline which creates a redacted copy for retention and discards raw input.
[01:24] Tara: Does the sanitization pipeline preserve length or token offsets? We have compliance tooling that relies on offsets.
[01:29] Priya: Good catch. Currently the sanitized copy is token-preserving but content-replaced with placeholders, e.g. <EMAIL_1>. So offsets are preserved for traceability but actual sensitive characters are replaced. There is an opt-in more aggressive mode that collapses fields which will not retain token offsets.
[01:45] Jules: Could you show the API example? We want per-request toggles from our ML microservice.
[01:49] Priya: Sure — in the docs you'll see request flags: "request_retention": "off|7d|90d", "redact_user_data": true/false, and "pii_masking_level": "standard|aggressive|custom". I'll paste a curl example in chat but I'll demo the SDK snippet too.
[02:04] [Priya shares screen, opens Console]
[02:12] Priya: Here's the toggle in Console — I toggle default to ephemeral 7d for this tenant. Under Scrubbing rules, I'm adding a custom regex to mask IBAN-like numbers they mentioned earlier, and a named-field rule for 'customer_ssn' so it gets replaced with <SSN_1>.
[02:29] Amira: How are named-field rules matched? Do you rely on JSON schema or form field names?
[02:34] Priya: You can match on request JSON keys or on inferred entities — if you pass a JSON payload with a key named 'ssn' we map it. There's also a heuristic entity extractor for free text. We log which rule triggered for auditability.
[02:45] Jules: And that log entry — will it contain the original value or just the rule id?
[02:49] Priya: It contains rule id and a hash of the original value (for de-dupe and trace) but never stores the raw sensitive string once scrubbing is applied. The hash uses a salted HMAC if you have your own KMS connected; otherwise it's Redwood-managed HMAC.
[03:02] Amira: OK, can the hashes be reversed if someone at Redwood wanted to?
[03:06] Priya: No. With customer KMS the salt key is customer-controlled so Redwood cannot derive originals. With default Redwood-managed keys, access is limited, but not available to front-line support unless with an approved escalation path documented in the DPA.
[03:18] Luis: We need full exportability for audits — can we export sanitized logs for 3rd-party auditors?
[03:23] Michael: Yes, we provide export APIs. You can request an export snapshot that contains only redacted records and the rule metadata. For Private deployments you can mount an S3 bucket to receive exports directly.
[03:34] Jules: Good. Now on legal we need the ability to turn off storage entirely via an API in case a data residency hold comes up — how fast is that effective?
[03:42] Priya: Turning request_storage to off is immediate for new requests; existing stored data requires a retention purge job which we can schedule — for ephemeral (7d) it'll prune automatically but you can request an immediate purge of the stored windows. For long retention there is a background purge which completes within 24 hours for typical volumes, but for enterprise customers we can offer expedited deletion SLA in the contract.
[04:03] Amira: Is there an immutable audit trail for deletion events? Our compliance team wants proof that data was wiped.
[04:09] Priya: Yes deletion events are themselves auditable — we record the operation, who triggered it, and a deletion confirmation token. The token is a digest of the purge job and timestamp. That entry is retained according to the audit-logs retention window (which is separate from request storage).
[04:21] Tara: You mentioned console UI and API parity — is there eventual consistency? If I change a scrubbing rule via API, how fast does the change take effect?
[04:29] Priya: Changes propagate within seconds to the scrubbing service; typically under 30s. For in-flight requests there is a short window where the pre-change rule may apply, so we recommend applying emergency rules via the "block_now" flag which rejects matching payloads during propagation.
[04:42] Jules: What about function/tool calling and structured outputs — any special handling?
[04:47] Priya: Structured outputs are treated as JSON payloads so field-level scrubs work reliably. For function outputs we recommend adding schema annotations so scrubs can match exactly.
[04:55] [Sound of typing — Michael pastes link to the data processing addendum]
[05:02] Michael: I'm dropping our DPA and SOC2 summary in chat. Also adding the KMS integration guide and the sample API calls.
[05:09] Amira: Thanks. One more: are logs egressed to third parties for benchmarking? We saw in other vendors that telemetry can be used for model improvement.
[05:17] Priya: Redwood does not share raw customer prompts with external model training unless you explicitly opt in via a separate data-use agreement. Telemetry used for platform improvements is aggregated and does not include raw prompts. That's in the DPA.
[05:29] Luis: Fine. A couple nitty gritty items — can we redact only specific keys and keep others? For example, keep transaction_amount but redact transaction_card_number.
[05:37] Priya: Yes that's the default use case — field-level allowlist/denylist. You can also define retention policies per field.
[05:43] Jules: For the POC we'd like request_storage default to off and then selectively enable 7d for specific routes. Can that be done via route-level policies?
[05:50] Priya: Absolutely. We have route policies where you can apply a policy by route ID or by model. We'll include the policy example in the shared repo.
[05:58] Tara: Does Redwood Optimize suggest scrubbing rules or just batching/cost suggestions?
[06:03] Priya: Redwood Optimize currently surfaces suggestions for quantization and batching, and for data handling it can recommend which fields to cache or strip based on frequency and token cost — it's an early feature but we can enable it for the POC. It will highlight high-risk fields based on heuristics.
[06:18] Jules: OK let's talk threat model a little — what happens if an operator misconfigures scrubbing rules and we end up leaking a field? Are there quick rollback or quarantine actions?
[06:27] Priya: We have a safety rollback flow: you can disable request storage, run a purge, and apply a quarantine policy that routes matching calls to a holding queue. Also there's a retroactive scrub job which will re-process stored records and redact them according to new rules. We log the scrub job output so auditors can verify what changed.
[06:42] Amira: That retroactive scrub — does it re-encrypt data with new KMS?
[06:46] Priya: Yes, re-encryption is supported; the job re-hashes and re-encrypts with the target key if you migrate keys. There's an audit hash chain so we can show lineage.
[06:56] Luis: Any limits on the number of custom regex rules? We have a long list.
[07:01] Priya: There's a soft limit of 2k rules per tenant for performance reasons; for enterprise accounts we can raise it and shard rules across rule groups.
[07:09] Jules: Do you have sample benchmark numbers for purge throughput? We're thinking of tens of terabytes in a worst case.
[07:15] Michael: We can pull logs from recent enterprise purges — typical throughput is a few TB/hour on shared infra; with Dedicated nodes we can reach tens of TB/hour and we can provide an SLA-backed plan. We'll include numbers in the follow-up.
[07:28] Tara: Can the export deliver directly to an on-prem SFTP instead of S3?
[07:33] Priya: Yes, export connectors can push to S3, GCS, or an SFTP endpoint. For private deployments we also support direct NFS mounts.
[07:41] [Clustered side talk, someone muted/unmuted]
[07:48] Amira: Quick question on the deletion audit token — is that token shared with the customer or only internally?
[07:53] Priya: We return the token to the caller (customer) so you can store it in your evidence trail; we also include it in the audit-log entry.
[07:59] Jules: Cool. Anything about rate limits affecting the scrubbing pipeline? We do high QPS on a few routes.
[08:06] Priya: Scrubbing is autoscaled; in hosted plans heavy scrubs can be offloaded to burst buckets or queued for async processing if you enable async_retention=true. For low-latency routes we recommend using allowlist scrubs (simple regex) and moving heavy entity-extraction scrubs to async.
[08:21] Luis: Will that affect latency? We can't have +200ms variability on critical routes.
[08:25] Priya: For synchronous scrubs the cost is sub-10ms for regex rules, ~20-80ms for ML entity extraction depending on payload size. Async mode adds no client latency but means raw payloads are in a short window before scrubbing; that's controlled by retention settings.
[08:40] Jules: All right — demo the SDK example now?
[08:44] Priya: Yep, here's a Node snippet. const resp = await redwood.run({ model: "redwood-large-v2", input: userMessage, request_retention: "7d", redact_user_data: true, pii_masking_level: "standard" }); This will apply tenant-level scrubs then request-level overrides.
[09:02] Tara: If redact_user_data=false at request and tenant is set to 7d, which wins?
[09:07] Priya: The most restrictive wins by default — policy precedence: route level -> request-level explicit -> tenant default. We log the effective policy for each call.
[09:17] Amira: We need that effective policy exposed in our logs for compliance, good.
[09:20] Michael: We'll include sample effective_policy output in the API example.
[09:25] [Priya navigates to audit log viewer]
[09:31] Priya: Here's the audit viewer — you can filter by rule id, by route, by user. This is paginated and you can export query results. Note the payload column shows redacted placeholders and the rule_trigger column shows which rule ran.
[09:45] Jules: Can we restrict who inside our org can see the export? Role-based access?
[09:51] Priya: Yes RBAC maps to SSO groups (SAML/Okta) and you can make a role that only allows audit-read or export-read.
[09:59] Amira: For legal reasons we might need to present the raw pre-scrub for a sealed e-discovery hold — is that possible?
[10:06] Priya: We do allow pre-scrub retrieval but only under strict conditions and with customer-managed key setup so that the raw content is encrypted with a key you control. That is gated by contract and logged heavily.
[10:18] Jules: OK — let's cover threat vectors: internal ops access, backup copies, and logs in backups. How do you ensure backups don't accidentally keep raw copies?
[10:26] Priya: Backups are run from sanitized datasets; raw payloads are not included in backups unless you opt into a specific backup mode for Private installations. For hosted, backups inherit tenant retention and scrubbing policies.
[10:36] Luis: Do you provide a SOC2 control mapping matrix for these features? Our auditors will ask which control covers purge validation etc.
[10:43] Michael: Yes — we'll send the SOC2 mapping doc that cross-walks to our features (retention purge, delete tokens, KMS, RBAC). It's in the security pack I'll drop.
[10:52] Tara: One operational question — mass rule changes across many tenants, is there a dry-run mode so we can see what would be scrubbed?
[10:59] Priya: We have a dry-run endpoint that returns sample matched entities and an estimated token impact. It doesn't mutate storage. Good for testing.
[11:08] Amira: Good. Any gotchas with function calling and attachments? We sometimes send base64-encoded attachments in prompts.
[11:14] Priya: Attachments are scanned but we recommend uploading attachments to a dedicated artifact store and reference them by ID in prompts to minimize risk. If you must send base64 in a prompt, add a custom scrub that matches that field name.
[11:27] Jules: Final item: can Redwood Optimize help reduce token exposure by suggesting which fields to strip or summarize?
[11:34] Priya: Yes, as I said earlier, Optimize can analyze recent traffic and recommend fields to strip, summarize, or cache. It can also generate a suggested scrubbing rule set you can import. It's alpha but we can enable it in the trial tenant.
[11:47] Michael: Ok let's recap next steps. We'll send SOC2 + DPA + KMS guide, provision a trial tenant with default request_storage=off and a route policy enabling 7d for test route, and schedule a security deep-dive. Priya will enable Optimize suggestions for the POC.
[12:03] Jules: That sounds good. Anyone else?
[12:06] Amira: No, thanks. We'll share the sensitive field list and sample payloads before Friday.
[12:11] Michael: Great — thanks all. We'll follow up via email with links and timeline.

End of recording.

Notes about transcription fidelity: small mis-hears present ("kay vee cache" for KV cache), occasional missing punctuation. Speaker turns are approximate.
